scenes.caption: Before 1952, investors mostly asked whether each stock was good.
In Portfolio Selection, Harry Markowitz argued that what matters is how holdings behave together.
Schematic: two risky assets that do not move in lockstep can combine into a portfolio less volatile than either alone.
His framing treated expected return and variance as the two things to trade off.
Diversification only helps when assets are not perfectly correlated, and correlations can rise exactly when markets are stressed.
Asset allocation is the split of your money between broad categories such as equity, debt, gold and cash.
Schematic: equity tends to swing more, debt tends to be steadier, and cash is stable but loses ground to inflation.
Illustration only: with ₹10 lakh, 70% equity and 30% debt moves far more in a bad year than 30% equity and 70% debt.
Choosing funds or stocks happens inside that split, so it usually has a smaller effect on your experience.
Illustration only: you estimate a business is worth ₹100 a share and insist on paying no more than ₹70.
A 20% error in your estimate still leaves you ahead of what you paid.
The gap is a buffer: your estimate may be wrong, the future may disappoint, or luck may turn.
It does not say the cheap thing is good. It says to price in your own fallibility before you commit money.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you gave up. It never appears on a bank statement.
Illustration only: ₹5 lakh earning 3% instead of a similar-risk 6% option forgoes about ₹15,000 a year.
The useful question is not 'is this good?' but 'is this better than what else I could do with the same money?'
It cuts both ways: compare alternatives net of trading costs, taxes and risk before concluding you are losing out.
Mr. Market names a price every day. His mood swings between euphoria and gloom, and his prices follow his mood.
Illustration only: steady profits, yet the price falls 25% in a month in a general sell-off. Only his mood changed.
Before trading, ask whether the price moved because of new facts about the asset or only because sentiment moved.
You are never obliged to trade. A quote is information about his mood, not a verdict on what your holding is worth.
On-call engineers limit how much any single failure can break: staged rollouts, canary releases, isolated services.
Illustration only: if a high-conviction idea goes to zero, Ravi loses 5% of his portfolio and Meera loses 40%.
A 50% fall needs a 100% gain to recover, so large losses are disproportionately costly.
Ask less 'how likely am I to be right?' and more 'if I am wrong, can I live with this loss?' Set a cap while calm.
Inside your circle of competence you can judge what something is worth. Outside it, you are guessing but may feel confident.
Buffett stressed that the circle's size matters less than knowing where its boundary lies.
A quick self-check: how it makes money, how it could lose, when you'd sell, its costs, and your real reason.
Schematic: one reasonable use of the idea is to size positions smaller the closer you are to the edge, and pass outside it.
Expected value: list the realistic outcomes, estimate how likely each is, multiply, and add.
Illustration only: a 60% chance of gaining ₹20,000 and a 40% chance of losing ₹25,000.
0.6 × 20,000 minus 0.4 × 25,000 is ₹2,000. A loss here would not prove the bet was bad.
A good decision can lose and a bad one can win. Judge the reasoning, not just the result; the odds are rough estimates.
Risk-adjusted return asks how much return you earned for each unit of risk you took.
William Sharpe's ratio divides return above a risk-free rate by the volatility of returns.
Illustration only: Fund A returns 12% with big swings; Fund B returns 10% with much smaller swings.
Schematic: per unit of volatility, B may rank higher, and B may also be easier to hold through a bad year.
Limits: volatility is only one definition of risk, and past ratios say little about the future. Ask better questions.
Being able to find the money is not the same as being able to get it fast.
Schematic: liquidity is how quickly and cheaply an asset becomes cash. Equity may be down 20% when needed; property takes months.
Without liquid reserves, a normal emergency becomes a forced sale of something you wanted to keep.
Check it: reachable within a day or two, stable in value, kept separate, months covered known, and 'emergency' defined.
The bucket approach sorts money by when you need it: near-term in safe assets, mid-term balanced, long-term in growth.
Supporters say buckets keep you calm in a crash. Critics say they are mental labels; one well-chosen mix does the same.
Both sides agree: money needed soon should not sit in volatile assets.
Evidence is balanced and thin either way. Editorial view: choose the structure you will actually follow. Education, not advice.
Risk tolerance is how much volatility you can stomach emotionally. Capacity is how much loss your finances can absorb.
Capacity depends on income stability, dependants, savings and time horizon.
Illustration only: Arjun is comfortable with big swings, but his family relies on his single salary and he has no reserve.
A sound plan respects the lower of the two. Boldness in a bull market is a poor guide to what you can afford to lose.
Once you own something, you seek, notice and remember what agrees with you, and the conviction feels stronger.
It feels like research but is mostly reassurance: agreeing posts get read, warnings get dismissed as noise.
Illustration only: a stock is down 30%. She reads posts calling the dip temporary and skips the report showing falling margins.
The fix is a different question: what evidence would change my mind, and have I looked for it?
In World War II, Wald's group was asked where to add armour to bombers, using bullet damage on returning planes.
Those were the survivors. Damage in other areas was probably fatal and was missing from the data.
Wald's insight: armour belonged where returning planes showed little damage.
Schematic: a fund list that omits closed or merged funds makes the average look better than what investors experienced.
Illustration only: you bought at ₹500 and it now trades at ₹350.
Anchoring: relying too heavily on an initial number. Waiting to break even ties your money to an old decision.
Whether to hold depends on future prospects and today's alternatives. Your entry price has no effect on those.
The right question: if you did not own it, would you buy it at ₹350 today?
Thaler called it mental accounting: sorting money into separate accounts, like salary, bonus and savings, each with its own rules.
Money is fungible: a rupee is a rupee. Yet a bonus or tax refund often gets spent more freely than the same salary.
Illustration only: Neha keeps ₹1 lakh in a deposit 'for emergencies' while paying a much higher rate on a credit card.
Labels can help, as with earmarked savings. The mistake is letting them override the arithmetic when the cost is large.
Others act, you copy, prices rise, and fear of missing out pushes the next person to act now.
Herding models show people can rationally follow earlier actors, so a crowd may rest on little independent judgement.
What independent reason, apart from other people buying, would you give for this purchase?
Before acting on a tip or trend, wait 48 hours and write down your own reason in one sentence.
